_comment: Every structural claim this project has made about a field, and what happened when it was tested under rule 18. The owner's requirement: the final Phase 2 report leads with this ledger, before any coverage number, because it says more about whether the dataset can be trusted than category counts do. A claim is only listed once it has been TESTED — an untested claim is not a finding and does not belong here. INWARD-FACING CLAIMS are tracked here too, and are the most dangerous class: a claim about our own criteria reads as introspection but is an empirical claim about the data. Two of the falsifications are of this kind, and both were live on the site.
_schema: status: falsified | survived. Each entry names the sub-areas, which were probed, what was found, and where the correction lives.

claims.claim: Marketing's independent practitioners publish in newsletters and blogs; the video supply is vendor-hosted.
claims.found: Alex Cattoni (848 uploads, a real copywriting curriculum), Pat Flynn (four 70-85 minute affiliate workshops) and 30 Minutes to President's Club all publish substantially in video. The standing note built on the claim was retired at 6/9, 67%.
claims.survives: The narrow form: Harry Dry has 4 uploads, Seth Godin 7, copyhackers and backlinko unresolvable, and the SEO end really is vendor-hosted.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: The standing note rendered on every marketing category page; verified live in a browser check at the time.

claims.claim: No usable first-aid teaching exists on video; the certifying bodies use YouTube for campaigns.
claims.found: PrepMedic, a critical-care flight paramedic with 353 uploads and 44 long-form bystander-first-aid videos, found on the first probe of the clinician end.
claims.survives: The institutional claim: certification needs hands-on assessment, so the bodies that certify treat the course as the product and video as its marketing.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal only. The gap lived in thin-gaps.json; the category was empty, which is not a claim, and the visitor-facing subject note said nothing false.

claims.found: Brand Master Academy: 39-63 minute interviews with April Dunford, Bobby Moesta, Blair Enns, Laura Ries.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal only — an unwritten conclusion that kept a category empty. Nothing was published.

claims.claim: practitioner, credentialed and cites-research are near-universal in some domains because of OUR inclusion rules — 'we do not list someone who explains a skill they have never practised'.
subAreas: whether any listed creator lacks the badge
whether the share is uniform across domains
claims.found: 29 of 196 creators carry no practitioner badge, so it is not a requirement. Measured across domains it runs 100% (marketing, business, fitness, programming, productivity) to 14% (philosophy). An inclusion rule would be near-uniform. credentialed runs 70% (relationships) to 0% (marketing); cites-research 71% (philosophy) to 0% (programming). All three track the subject, not our preference.
claims.survives: A real but secondary editorial preference for qualifications in relationships, which is why that one entry is 'mixed' rather than 'field'.
claims.correctionIn: data/domain-notes.json corrected — 15 entries reclassified and moved to category pages; the colophon section rewritten
claims.note: The worst of the four: never probed at all when made, repeated in every batch report from 17 to 25, and shipped to visitors as a claim about our own rigour.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: On the colophon, as a statement about our own rigour, for several weeks.

claims.claim: Independent, credentialed, educational addiction content is genuinely scarce.
claims.found: The clinician end is ASAM: 49 uploads, archived since February 2021, conference plenaries addressed to physicians. Five other clinician handles do not resolve.

claims.claim: No conversion-optimization teaching catalogue exists on video.
claims.found: All four probed before the claim was written — the first gap documented in the right order. Nudgestock recorded as a near-miss and not mapped: adjacent subject, not the same one.

claims.claim: No credible critic of the relationship-advice field exists on video.
subAreas: credentialed clinicians critiquing the content industry
claims.found: Mickey Atkins is the near-miss — credentialed, with a substantive Dr. Amen debunk — but her critical work is a small part of a catalogue that is mostly reality-television commentary, so the slot would be thin. Rule 11 applies.
claims.survives: The claim, on rule 11 grounds rather than absence.

claims.claim: No credible critic of commercialised philosophy exists on video.
claims.found: Philosophy Tube read rather than counted: 15 of 50 recent uploads over twenty minutes, but the subject is political and social essay, not criticism of philosophy content.

claims.claim: A creator appears under a skill only when their work supports it — typically two to four skills, never more than six. (Stated on the colophon to visitors, and as the default in rule 4.)
claims.madeAt: phase 1 brief, shipped on the colophon in batch 22
subAreas: the actual distribution of mappings per creator
whether the design intent was ever met
claims.found: The median is 1 and the mean 1.47. 62% of creators have exactly ONE mapping; only 38% fall in the claimed two-to-four band. The ratio was measured at 1.58 back at 143 creators and has DRIFTED DOWN since — so the claim got steadily more wrong and was never re-run.
claims.survives: The 'never more than six' half, and the scope rule itself. 2-4 was always a design intent in rule 4, not a description of the dataset; the error was restating an intent to visitors as a fact.
claims.correctionIn: js/views/colophon.js — the rule now says most appear under one, and the coverage section computes the median rather than asserting it
claims.note: Second inward-facing claim to fail, and the same shape as the badge one: cheap to query, never queried.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: On the colophon, in the inclusion rules a visitor reads to decide whether to trust the list.

claims.claim: The site keeps two things in your browser: plan progress, and whether you dismissed the survey question.
claims.found: Five distinct stores, not two: theme preference, plan progress, categories seen this session, whether the form endpoint exists, and the survey dismissal state. I grepped localStorage when writing the sentence and never looked at sessionStorage — the same partial-search error as the outward findings, at the smallest possible scale, one exchange after naming the pattern.
claims.survives: That nothing leaves the device and nothing reaches us. Both still true.
claims.correctionIn: index.html footer now names the kinds and states no count; validate.mjs holds a registry and fails on any undisclosed store
claims.note: Caught by the enforcement written in the same batch, not by review. The check found its author's error within minutes of existing.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: In the site footer, in the paragraph about what we collect.

claims.claim: The falling marginal mapping ratio was partly a search artefact of single-target fills, and the depth pass would push it back up as categories filled out.
subAreas: whether single-target fills were depressing the measured ratio
whether a depth pass can produce a ratio above 1.0 at all
probedWhenMade: whether single-target fills were depressing the measured ratio
claims.found: Batches 33-43 ran at a 1.08 marginal ratio across 25 creators — lower than when the claim was made, not higher. The reason was available without any measurement: a depth pass names one thin category and fills it with a specialist who legitimately belongs only there, and rule 4's double-counting test forbids the second mapping that would lift the ratio. A depth pass yields 1.00 by construction. The mechanism was knowable before the prediction was made; I checked the first sub-area and asserted the second.
claims.survives: Nothing of the prediction. The narrower observation it rested on stands: single-target fills do measure at 1.00, which is why the ratio fell. That was the mechanism, not an artefact obscuring one.
claims.correctionIn: Depth target restated from 3 to 2 in scripts/validate.mjs and CLAUDE.md; the arithmetic that settles it recorded with the change. Headroom past depth 2 now allocated by scripts/lib/depth3.mjs rather than by whichever category is being researched.
claims.note: SECOND PROJECTION OF THIS KIND. The first was 'depth 5 everywhere is reachable at 400 creators', restated to 3 at batch 32 and now to 2. Both were forecasts about our own process rather than about YouTube, and both were made without testing the mechanism that drives the number. The owner's ruling: a prediction about our own process belongs in this ledger alongside claims about it — same class, same standard. Consequence for the live estimate: a 31-batch projection for the remaining 172 creators is recorded in UNVERIFIED.md explicitly discounted on this record.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal only. The depth number has never appeared in visitor-facing copy; the colophon computes what the data actually shows rather than stating a target, which is the rule-18 fix from batch 26 doing its job.

claims.claim: Contrast is verified by script, not by eye: 22 text/background pairings across both themes, all passing WCAG AA.
claims.found: No such script has ever existed in this repository. `git log --all --name-only` has no record of any contrast, a11y or colour-checking file being added OR deleted — it was never there. The number 22 came from nowhere that can be identified.
claims.survives: The substance, once an artifact was built to test it: 0 pairings below WCAG AA. The count did not — 30, not 22.
claims.correctionIn: scripts/check-contrast.mjs written and run; the sentence in CLAUDE.md now names the script and carries the number the script prints.
claims.note: WORSE THAN THE BADGE CLAIM, and a different kind of worse. The badge claim was a wrong inference from real data. This asserted a specific measured result about our own rigour with no measurement anywhere behind it — it was never even wrong, because nothing ever produced it. It also survived every previous sweep: the rule-18 ledger looks for claims that were tested and failed, and this one could not be tested. It took asking a different question — which rules require manual repetition — to surface it. Its own first run then reported two failures that were phantoms, because it tested semantic tokens that no CSS rule uses. The owner's addition, and it is the more important half: the sibling instance — '79% of every record is hand-written prose' — was not merely a wrong number. It was the STATED REASON the bottleneck was prose rather than quota, and that framing shaped weeks of decisions about pace, batch size and where effort went. Nobody questioned it because it sounded measured. A strategic conclusion resting on a measurement that never existed is worse than a false badge on a card, and it survived precisely because nothing about it looked like a claim.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal. But it is the claim most likely to have been repeated to someone as evidence of care.

claims.claim: 79% of every record is hand-written prose — therefore the bottleneck is the writing and the reading, not the quota.
subAreas: whether the conclusion it supported holds
claims.found: No script has ever computed a prose share. Measured directly at batch 45: 65% of record bytes, and the denominator moves every time a structured field is added — `catalogue` and `entity` both landed the same day.
claims.survives: The conclusion, on other evidence. Batch 43 spent ~38 recalled handle probes and seven evidence dumps for three creators, which showed the bottleneck was candidate generation rather than either prose or quota. The conclusion outlived the number that was given as its reason.
claims.correctionIn: CLAUDE.md now states 65% and names the measurement; data/claim-artifacts.json requires every number about ourselves to name its producer.
claims.note: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ENTRY IN THIS LEDGER, and not because the number was far out. It was load-bearing: cited as the reason the bottleneck was prose, it shaped pace and batch-size decisions for weeks. It was never challenged because it sounded like the output of a measurement. That is the signature of this class — the claims that look most settled are the ones nothing produced.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal, and the wrong place to look for its cost. Its cost was in decisions, not in copy.

claims.claim: Query-based discovery plus batching the reading across categories should support 5-6 creators per batch, cutting the remaining work to roughly 23 batches.
subAreas: whether discovery finds creators recall misses
probedWhenMade: whether discovery finds creators recall misses
claims.found: Discovery-sourced batches 44-45 ran at 2.50 creators/batch. The one purely recall-sourced batch since, 46, ran at 3.00. Batches 33-43 ran at 2.27. There is no rate difference: 5-6/batch was never observed at any point in the project's history under any method, and I offered it as a projection with a mechanism attached rather than a measurement.
claims.survives: The narrower and real benefit, which was the part I actually tested. Discovery finds creators recall does not: all three of batch 44 came from it after two prior health batches of recall had not produced them, and it returned @sameerislammd when three recalled handle guesses had all missed. It changes WHICH creators are findable, not HOW MANY per batch.
claims.correctionIn: CLAUDE.md now carries one rate — the measured 2.36/batch — and no optimistic figure. The 23-batch target is withdrawn.
claims.note: THIRD PACE PROJECTION, THIRD FAILURE, and the pattern across all three is identical: I measured the mechanism (single-target fills yield 1.00; discovery surfaces unseen candidates) and then asserted a rate the mechanism was supposed to produce, without measuring the rate. The mechanism claim was true every time. The rate claim was wrong every time. The owner has discounted each of these on the record; the correct response is to stop offering the optimistic half at all, not to discount it harder.
claims.reachedVisitorsNote: Internal. Its cost is in planning, like the 79%.

_framing: How to state this ledger, per the owner: the honest framing is that this project tested N of its own claims and found M wrong — and the alternative was NOT M correct claims, it was M wrong ones nobody checked. BOTH NUMBERS ARE COMPUTED FROM THIS FILE, never typed: the paragraph read "six" for eight batches after the count had moved past six, which is the inward-facing class of rule 18 appearing inside rule 18ʼs own report. Report both numbers together: how many were falsified, and how many had REACHED VISITORS before being caught. The second is the difference between an internal process finding its own errors and a dataset that shipped them.

whatTheChecksCaught.note: The clearest evidence the automated checks paid for themselves, to be cited in the final report.
whatTheChecksCaught.case: At batch 36, five stored domain-note measurements had drifted as the dataset grew — fitness/sells-course 14/15 to 17/18, programming/practitioner 14/14 to 25/25, programming/sells-course 10/14 to 15/25, fitness/practitioner 15/15 to 18/18, tech/practitioner 9/11 to 10/12.
whatTheChecksCaught.whoCaughtIt: All five by the validator. NONE by review — and they were reviewed, in the same session, by someone actively watching for exactly this.
whatTheChecksCaught.contrast: This is the badge-claim failure mode caught in one pass instead of nine batches. The badge claim was the same kind of error — a stored assertion the data had moved past — and it survived nine batches of careful reading because nothing queried it.

_classes._comment: Three distinct failures live in this ledger and they need different defences. Named at batch 45 on the owner's instruction, after the third was found.
_classes.stale-stored-fact: A fact was true when written and stopped being queried. Defence: re-query it on a schedule. Six instances — the handle list, the badge shares, five drifted domain measurements, the duplicate record, entry-video titles, size bands.
_classes.schema-cannot-express-it: The value was wrong the DAY it was written, because the field's shape could not carry the truth. Defence: write the truest sentence about a real subject, then try to say it in the schema. Two instances — `status` could not say 'quiet for eighteen months'; `role` could not say 'this is a company'.
_classes.never-even-wrong: A claim that no process ever produced. Not stale, not mis-shaped — there was never an artifact behind it, so it could not have been checked, and its specific number came from nowhere at all. Defence: for every measurement asserted about ourselves, name the artifact that computes it, or delete the number. See data/claim-artifacts.json. THIS IS THE HARDEST OF THE THREE, and the owner's framing is the right one: the other instances were checkable and unchecked, this one had nothing to check against. Rule 18 looks for claims that were tested and failed, so a claim no process ever produced is invisible to it by construction — it took changing the question, to 'which rules require manual repetition', to surface this one at all. The defence cannot be a better test; it has to be a requirement at the point of writing: name the artifact in the same sentence as the number.
